fields.title: Physics
fields.subtitle: Push a cart. Connect motion, rates and energy.
assumptions: A point mass travels on a straight horizontal track with constant acceleration. Position starts at zero; speed and acceleration are nonnegative.
The first stage deliberately sets acceleration to zero. Later stages restore the chosen acceleration. Energy is translational kinetic energy; friction and rotation are omitted.

stages.title: Distance
stages.headline: How far does the cart go?
stages.action: Move time. Each extra second adds the same distance.
stages.why: At constant speed, distance is the size of each one-second step multiplied by the number of steps. The graph slope has units m/s.
stages.question: Explain why doubling time doubles distance in this stage.

stages.title: Velocity
stages.headline: Make the cart speed up.
stages.action: Raise acceleration. Watch the velocity graph tilt.
stages.formula: v(t) = v₀ + at; x(t) = v₀t + ½at²
stages.why: Acceleration adds the same amount to velocity each second. Differentiating position gives velocity; differentiating velocity gives acceleration.
stages.question: Why does position become quadratic even though velocity is a straight line?

stages.title: Energy
stages.headline: Speed has a squared cost.
stages.action: Change the starting speed. Compare the final speed and energy.
stages.formula: K = ½mv², with v = v₀ + at
stages.why: Kinetic energy uses the final speed, not just the starting speed. Doubling final speed multiplies energy by four when mass stays fixed.
stages.question: Why does doubling the starting speed not necessarily quadruple the final energy when the same push continues?

stages.title: Area → distance
stages.headline: Read distance from velocity.
stages.action: Move time. The shaded area is the distance traveled.
stages.why: The rectangle contributes v₀t and the triangle contributes ½at². Both multiply m/s by s, giving meters.
stages.question: Show how the rectangle and triangle together recover the position formula.

fields.title: Mechanical engineering
fields.subtitle: Trade speed for torque. Store work in a spring.
assumptions: The input gear has 12 teeth. Both gears share tooth size, do not slip, and have no losses. Reported speeds and torques are magnitudes; meshing external gears turn in opposite directions.
The spring is a separate ideal linear spring with stiffness 120 N/m. Compression stays within this assumed linear range; no real component rating is implied.

stages.title: Speed ratio
stages.headline: Make a slower, stronger gear pair.
stages.action: Add teeth to the output gear. Watch its speed fall.
stages.why: The same number of teeth passes the contact each second. A gear with three times as many teeth needs three times as long for one revolution.
stages.question: If output speed halves, what changed about the gear ratio?

stages.title: Torque
stages.headline: Trade turning speed for turning force.
stages.action: Raise the input torque. Follow the output torque.
stages.why: The same contact force acts at different pitch radii. A larger output radius produces more torque, while its angular speed is smaller.
stages.question: Why does extra output torque not mean the gear created extra power?

stages.title: Power
stages.headline: Keep the energy accounting honest.
stages.action: Raise input rpm. Both power bars must stay equal.
stages.why: A revolution is 2π radians and a minute is 60 seconds. Converting rpm before multiplying by torque gives watts. Ideal input and output power agree.
stages.question: Explain why using rpm directly in P = Tω gives the wrong units and number.

stages.title: Spring work
stages.headline: Store energy by compressing a spring.
stages.action: Compress the spring. The shaded triangle is stored work.
stages.why: Force grows from zero to kx, so average force is half the final force. Work is the triangular area under the force graph.
stages.question: Why is the work ½kx² instead of kx²?

fields.title: Electrical engineering
fields.subtitle: Control current. Charge a tiny energy store.
assumptions: An ideal DC source and constant resistor are used; temperature effects, wire resistance and component limits are omitted.
The RC stage starts with an uncharged ideal capacitor. Capacitance is entered in microfarads and converted to farads; resistance times capacitance is measured in seconds.

stages.title: Current
stages.headline: Give charge a push.
stages.action: Raise voltage. Watch current grow through the resistor.
stages.why: At fixed resistance, current is proportional to voltage. The readout converts amperes to milliamperes by multiplying by 1000.
stages.question: If voltage doubles while resistance stays fixed, what happens to current?

stages.title: Heating
stages.headline: Resistance changes the energy flow.
stages.action: Increase resistance while keeping source voltage fixed.
stages.why: At fixed voltage, raising resistance reduces current and power. The statement would differ if a current source held current fixed.
stages.question: Why must you say what is held fixed before comparing resistor heating?

stages.title: Charging
stages.headline: A capacitor fills gradually.
stages.action: Move time. Compare capacitor voltage with the source.
stages.why: As the capacitor voltage grows, less voltage remains across the resistor, so charging slows. At one time constant RC, the capacitor reaches about 63.2% of source voltage.
stages.question: Why does this graph approach the source voltage instead of rising in a straight line forever?

fields.title: Architecture & civil engineering
fields.subtitle: Span a gap. Balance loads. Explore stiffness.
assumptions: A uniform rectangular beam is simply supported at both ends and loaded at its center. The illustrative elastic modulus is fixed at 11 GPa.

The bending model assumes small deflection, linear elasticity and negligible shear deformation. Beam self-weight and capacity checks are omitted. Deflection is visually exaggerated and is not a structural design or safety assessment.

stages.title: Materials
stages.headline: How much material spans the gap?
stages.action: Lengthen the beam. Track its material volume.
stages.why: The cross-sectional area is fixed in this stage. Each extra meter adds one more identical slice of material.
stages.question: Which dimensions must stay fixed for volume to be proportional to span?

stages.title: Balance
stages.headline: Share the load between supports.
stages.action: Increase the central load. Watch both reactions grow.
stages.formula: R_left + R_right = F; R_left = R_right = F/2
stages.why: Vertical force balance gives the sum. Symmetry, or a moment equation about one end, gives equal shares for a central load.
stages.question: Why would moving the load away from the center destroy the equal split?

stages.title: Stiffness
stages.headline: Depth is more powerful than it looks.
stages.action: Increase beam depth. Watch the predicted bend shrink.
stages.why: Depth appears cubed in the second moment of area. With load, width and span fixed, doubling depth divides this model’s deflection by eight.
stages.question: Compare doubling depth with doubling width: why do their effects differ?

fields.title: Finance
fields.subtitle: Grow a savings plan. Separate dollars from buying power.
assumptions: The initial balance is $1000. Interest compounds once per year at a constant hypothetical rate; contributions arrive at each year’s end.
Taxes, fees and changing returns are omitted. Purchasing power divides the future balance by a constant price-growth factor; this is an arithmetic scenario, not a forecast or recommendation.

stages.title: Time
stages.headline: Give growth more years.
stages.action: Extend the timeline. Compare growth with the money added.
stages.why: Each year, interest applies to the existing balance before that year’s contribution is added. The lower reference line shows only the money put in.
stages.question: Why does the balance curve bend while the contribution-only line stays straight?

stages.title: Rate
stages.headline: A percentage acts on a changing base.
stages.action: Change the annual rate. Watch repeated growth compound.
stages.why: Repeated multiplication acts on the whole previous balance. The plotted scenario also includes your chosen year-end contributions; the no-contribution formula isolates the growth mechanism.
stages.question: How is compounding different from adding the same interest amount every year?

stages.title: Contributions
stages.headline: Build the plan one deposit at a time.
stages.action: Increase the yearly deposit. Earlier deposits have longer to grow.
stages.why: The last deposit gets no interest yet; the first gets n−1 years. At a zero rate, the geometric sum becomes n, so the balance is simply B₀+nC.
stages.question: Explain why the deposit sum ends at exponent n−1, not n.

stages.title: Buying power
stages.headline: The same dollars may buy less.
stages.action: Raise inflation. Compare future dollars with today’s buying power.
stages.why: The future balance and the price level both grow. Dividing by the price multiplier converts the entire future balance into current purchasing units.
stages.question: Why is subtracting i dollars from the balance not an inflation adjustment?
